faq.a: In flexion the ACL is less taut, so the PCL bears most of the posterior load, preventing the tibia from slipping backward.
faq.q: Why does the PCL become more important when the knee is flexed?

faq.a: Low‑grade (grade I‑II) tears often respond to bracing and physiotherapy; high‑grade (grade III) tears may need reconstruction, especially in active patients.
faq.q: Can a PCL injury heal without surgery?

faq.a: Posterior drawer tests translation actively; posterior sag is a static observation of tibial sag when the knee is relaxed, both indicating PCL laxity.
faq.q: What is the difference between a posterior drawer and a posterior sag sign?

exam: A patient presents after a motor‑vehicle collision with posterior knee pain and a positive posterior drawer – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a stress lateral X‑ray to quantify posterior translation when MRI is unavailable.

How does the anatomy of the PCL explain its resistance to posterior tibial translation? — Its origin on the femur and broad insertion on the posterior tibial plateau create a tether that opposes backward movement.

What clinical features differentiate an isolated PCL injury from combined ACL‑PCL trauma? — Isolated PCL shows a normal anterior drawer and Lachman test; combined injury shows both anterior and posterior laxity.
In a low‑resource hospital without MRI, how would you grade a PCL tear? — Use the posterior drawer test and stress X‑ray; grade I (<5 mm), II (5‑10 mm), III (>10 mm) translation.

Why is the popliteal artery at risk in posterior knee injuries, and what sign alerts you? — The artery lies directly posterior to the PCL; a rapidly expanding posterior swelling or loss of distal pulse signals vascular injury.
What rehabilitation principle is crucial after a grade II PCL tear? — Early controlled range‑of‑motion with a posterior‑stabilising brace, avoiding posterior loading for 6‑8 weeks.
When would you choose surgical reconstruction of the PCL in a young athlete? — Persistent instability after 3‑6 months of rehab, grade III tear, or combined multiligament injury.
How does a posterior tibial slope affect PCL stress and injury risk? — Increased posterior slope augments shear forces on the PCL, raising the likelihood of rupture.
ai.title: Posterior Cruciate Ligament
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) anchors the tibia to the femur, preventing posterior translation of the tibia and stabilising the knee in flexion. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose and manage knee injuries, especially where imaging is limited.

b: Works with ACL to control anteroposterior motion
sections.p: The PCL is one of two cruciate ligaments that cross inside the knee joint. It is the strongest ligament of the knee and is essential for posterior stability, especially when the knee is flexed.
The PCL originates from the anterolateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle and inserts on the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, just distal to the posterior tibial plateau.

b: Anterior to posterior horn of medial meniscus
sections.p: Within the intercondylar notch the PCL lies anterior to the posterior horn of the medial meniscus and posterior to the ACL. The popliteal artery and vein run just posterior to the ligament.
The PCL receives blood from branches of the middle genicular artery, a branch of the popliteal artery.
Sensory innervation is via the posterior articular branches of the tibial nerve.
The PCL prevents posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur and contributes to rotational stability, especially when the knee is flexed beyond 30°.

b: Common mechanism: dashboard injury, fall on flexed knee
Isolated PCL rupture is rare; often combined with other ligament damage
May present with posterior knee pain, swelling, and a positive posterior drawer test
sections.p: PCL injuries usually result from a posteriorly directed force on a flexed knee (e.g., dashboard injury). In low‑resource settings they may be missed without MRI; a careful exam is essential.

t.b: Is the tibia translating posteriorly compared with the opposite knee? → Positive test indicates PCL laxity

t.a: Knee X‑ray (AP & lateral) with stress view
t.b: Is there increased posterior tibial translation (>6 mm) on lateral view? → Confirms significant PCL injury when MRI unavailable
Does the ligament appear discontinuous or thinned? → Gold standard for grading injury

b: Posterior drawer: patient supine, knee flexed 90°, push tibia posteriorly
Compare side‑to‑side translation; >6 mm difference is abnormal
Check for associated injuries: meniscus, PLC, neurovascular status
sections.p: When evaluating a knee trauma patient, always assess both cruciates. A positive posterior drawer with a stable anterior drawer points toward isolated PCL injury.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe knee instability with inability to bear weight
Rapidly expanding knee swelling suggesting vascular injury
Neurovascular deficit (loss of sensation or pulse distal to knee)
